Do you like paper? Hate people? This is the game for you! This thrilling, hyper-realistic paper pushing game includes miles and miles of paper-handling. From manuals, to passports, to municipally-issued identification slips, to photo-ids, to so much more! Not just paper, though; stamps. That's right, you get to STAMP your papers. Red and green colors! But mostly the red. Well, if you like the color red, it's a plus!
Not only that, you get the hate of an entire population (or so it feels) directed at you for denying them passage into the glorious Arstotzka. And you get to hate them back by denying them even more, those filthy heathens!

Well, to wrap this up in a way those who don't like reading will understand, (TL;DR:) 'Papers, Please' is a great game. Especially if you like paper.
Despite just being about checking passports, I had a lot of fun. Has a great story and multiple moments that are actually fun and different.
I unironically find endless mode to be more entertaining than the story mode. Not because the story is bad, it's really good, but I just wanna keep checking people in lmao.

Government Admin Simulator 1982.

Or, that is how it would be if this game weren't addictive, engrossing and filled with misery everywhere you look.

You are a lowly citizen given the opportunity to admit people into the country. You need to be alert for any problems with their documents, a typo here, the height of the person, anything can be wrong, and you need a sharp eye.

Having worked in admin before make me realise it's easier when you've done this kind of focused examination of documents to ensure the people have everything they need.

Pre-scripted events like terrorism, bombs, a secret government organisation, bribes from applicants, favours from officials appear to make you question the orders you receive from above, along with potential opportunities to give your family a better home. And yes, you do have a family, though you don't see them, you need to inspect enough people each day to earn money for rent, food, heat, and medicine etc when needed.

Multiple endings, so plenty of chances to get it wrong or right. Overall, a very well made game which harkens back to the era of the fall of the Soviet union, East and West Germany and the breakup of Yugoslavia.
This is a very good game, the options of being a civil servant or obeying the government at certain times really makes you question everything.

This is a game I quit half-way through, probably never will play again, but yet recommend strongly.

As a foreword, bear in mind that I am an oversensitive wuss that gets uncomfortable by the random killing I commit when I play a GTA game.

The game puts you at the forefront of the misery and violence of the modern world : the visa check-in. It will resonnate strongly with whoever had to be familiar with such situation.
Fellow reviewer Brandon Cackowski-Schnell stated on multiple occasions he was amazed and scared at how the game turned him into a robotic mostly uncaring machine, just to protect those dear to him. In my case, the reaction was the exact opposite : I couldn't cope with the harshness of the job and so I did what I love to think I would have done in real life in such a position : I quit. (Please don't ask my in-game relatives what happened of them ;)

In that sense, as Dark Souls, I think it truly can be the closest you can get to a real role-playing game on a computer.
Incredible experience. There is no game like it that I've played. Definitely worth your time.

A nice little indie game about being a boarder patrol gaurd checking passports in a comunist country. Has good moral and gameplay complexities for a game made by one person. Check it out if you like games that you can play just to pass the time.

For such a small indie game (in every aspect, particularly file size), this is one of the most engrossing games I've ever played. A perfect balance between puzzle solving while also making serious moral choices. Plenty of tongue-in-cheek allusions to Cold War Communism. The Story Mode can be completed in 5 hours or less, which may turn off people who desire longer-running games. However, the replay value is going through the story again and making different choices to achieve different endings. Once you get the "Glory to Arstotzka" ending, you'll receive the code for the "Endless" game mode, where you can play to earn a place on global leaderboards. For a $9.99 game, it's worth every penny.

If I could recommend this game 1000 times, I would. A statement to how much I love this game is that this is my first ever review! Papers, Please is basically a desk job simulation game. I know to some that may not sound like loads of fun, but somehow this game made me feel like I didn't want to dissapoint it. It envokes frustration when your heart is racing while waiting to see if you made a mistake and are about to get a citation. It makes you feel guilty for not letting in every immigrant that begs you even though they don't have the proper paperwork. You feel guilty (sometimes) for letting your poor mother in law stay cold because you can't afford heat that day. The game is fairly easy to get the hang of once you start memorizing the rules, but to me it didn't feel like it was repetitive (even though you truly are doing the same thing over and over for 31 days.) The difficulty does get harder as the game continues. The story and quirky characters kept it from feeling repetitive. 10/10 would buy this game over and over. I love you Jorji! You funny guy.

This is an older game but a fun one. You are an immigration agent who is assessing people's papers and deciding if they are genuine. You'll have guides that tell you the correct features of papers from certain areas, and there will be more and more things you have to verify. The person will provide you a name, origin country, etc. and you'll have to scour the paperwork for errors/frauds. Some of them will be wanted criminals (according to the totalitarian regime running things) and you have to decide their fate. You will need a VERY GOOD attention to detail to succeed and the game is very challenging because you're trying to review as many people's papers as you can by day, but making errors is VERY costly and get just a few and you're broke and done. With practice, you may get better, but at first reviewing all the reference pages is TOUGH. There are around 20 different endings so your choices and success will determine the outcome and this adds replayability value. The game comes from a while ago, so check security. It has basic pixelated graphics, and touches on the macabre. Recommend for very detail-oriented people or to build those kind of skills. 7/10
Only played it through once but I would definitely do it again. Just waiting for the urge to strike... almost like reading a book taking place at a border office.

The game touches on the right themes.
Pros
Sound: Good audio effects and voice acting; it's really nice to hear that.
Endings: Many endings with unpredictable conclusions; the game has about 20 different endings.
Choices: You have to make moral choices throughout the whole game. You can choose a side in this game.
Gameplay Curve: The difficulty curve increases as you progress through the game. New features and gameplay changes are introduced.
Cons
Difficulty: If you are a newbie, you might struggle with it. You should select easy mode.
Boredom: Sometimes, it can be boring to play for a long time.
In conclusion: Papers, Please is a good game with an advanced lore (consider referencing the short film). It is highly recommended to play if you have never played it before.

It's a fun game but it gets repetitive after some time. Finishing a day takes a very long time especially if you want to get all endings. You can't select a certain route for an ending at most times, you have to start from an earlier point and grind your way back up which takes a lot of time. The most annoying "feature" is when you alt tab the game pauses itself making it impossible to wait the day out while doing something else. It's really frustrating and you can't disable it in the options.

Effortlessly mixing emergent storytelling, a thrilling core narrative, a fairly unique puzzle gameplay style and a rich but despondent atmosphere. If Dust: An Elysian Tail is the sort of game I could see myself making, Papers Please is the game I WISH I could make; one where every single moving part is in working order, flowing beautifully and creating a system where I honestly can't think of anything you could or should take out or even tweak. It's an entity unto itself but will stand up for years to come. Highly recommended for enthusiasts and "casuals" alike.

This is a fantastic game that shows the dehumanizing process of strict immigration policy, and showcases how everyone suffers, including the player, who is in charge and holds in their fate the lives of these very ordinary people. There is a certain point in the game where yeah, you're getting good at your job, but you're always thinking, "surely, there is a better way to do this."

This is a brilliant game that can be virtually played on every single system, and I find it has aged like fine wine in terms of its timeliness.

"Papers, Please" is a game with logic, memorization, and observation puzzles but not in the way most people would expect. The solution to these puzzles involve meticulous readings of passports, government documents, and other miscellaneous pieces of identification. What is interesting is that these puzzles may look boring on "paper" but in execution, they elevate the game to artistic heights that few indie games can reach. This is all thanks to the game's story which is both fascinating and depressing due to the real world implications.

Playing as an immigration officer for the fictional country of Arstotzka, the fate of countless strangers depends on both your skill and judgment. There will be instances where you must choose whether or not to be charitable to the needy or loyal to your family & country. How the player chooses to make these decisions is done entirely through the game's mechanics and not through a quick time event or cutscene. Though the gameplay is simple, the story is intriguing enough to prevent monotony. Due to the fact that the size of your pay depends on your speed and precision, there is a constant pressure to improve and maintain. With that much burden surrounding the player, is there any time left to think about personal morals?
This game is lots of fun especially if you have a short attention span. you are constantly trying to remember the rules and read the content of the papers. Lots of fun I highly recommend.

Wonderful game with simple graphics, so you can still play this on your potato from 1997.

Surprisingly engaging story and characters for a game about cross-referencing descrepancies in passports! Also makes you question morality more than it has any right to as you make choices in regard to bending some rules or not.

After playing this game, I can now sympathize with border guards who take too long (fear of getting it wrong), detain people for little reason (bonuses for bread on the table) and even those who seem to relish in confiscating passports (you just fell cool.) That doesn't I want them to do it, I just see why they do. Anyway. TENADDATEN.

Amazing game It's full of depth and has you thinking about the process of immigration and the border. The art is amazing and the characters you interact with are engaging. I loved playing this! It didn't feel too long or too short. There are different endings to it as well and an endless mode, so this definitely has replay-ability which is nice. Overall, a really great game!
A game about paperwork that turns out to be one of the most significant and thought-provoking games of the 21st century. 10/10.

I only picked this game up since Zero Punctuation's Yahtzee recommended it. After all, what sane person would get tingly below the belt for what is essentially a paperwork simulator? Well I would for one. Begin the story mode and you immediately have to start working to earn enough to support you're family you've never met while being careful enough not to get cited, fired, or imprisoned! And as simple as that may seem, there are so many possible things to watch out for, and so little instruction, that you will mess up completely on you're first run. Combine that with the high stakes for you and your family and you've got plenty of tension and atmosphere. Also the constant oppresive music is a nice touch.

Really fun if you like to be in excrutiating pain in 6 minute increments

Papers, Please's innovation on gaming is so crazy no one even knows what genre you would call it. I'd call it flippin' awesome. It's so great, passport not required!

The game is very original, and the concept is really interesting, with some really nice details, and for the first hour or two you will probably have lots of fun playing as the border guard dude.

However, after that the game offers nothing new or suprising, doesn't really reward you in any way, and becomes a bit tedious to play. Replayability is close to nonexistant, in my opinion.

The game ain't THAT expensive especially if it is on discount, so you might as well try it out... the game is REALLY original after all, and deserves some of the good reviews.. but don't expect much of a gaming experience after the fun of the first few hours has worn off.

It's an interesting take on public relations with other nations. To describe it as simply a day in the life of border security would probably sound stupid. But it's all the people you interact with as you go about it that makes it so interesting.
Papers, Please is a mindblowing game, so deep yet so simple. It's a demonstration of what makes videogames such a beautfiul medium.

Very fun little game! If you enjoy minute details and are good at pattern recognition, you'll have a great time with it.
You can get a decent few hours of gameplay out of it, and there are several endings based on your choices, so it has pretty good replayability. Solid 8.5/10. Glory to Arstotzka o7
